Same tier, same provider, release over release: the number that actually shows up on your bill is going the opposite way from the headlines.
By Aemond & Ivan, Morph

Press enter or click to view image in full size

ChatGPT launched on November 30, 2022, and for a while it felt like the whole industry was standing in line for the same ride. Free trial, constant “at capacity” errors, a queue that never seemed to shrink. That scramble — Claude’s website buckling on a big release day, DeepSeek’s server errors on launch, Gemini throwing 529s when a region’s shared compute pool runs dry — is a demand signal you can’t fake. When that many people want in at once, price is usually the thing that has to give.
[Aemond: what strikes me editing this is how quickly “the model is down” stopped sounding like a bug report and started sounding like a capacity problem — that’s usually the tell that an industry is about to start charging differently for the same thing.]
And it has. Just maybe not in the direction most people assume.
The “everything’s getting cheaper” story is true — and it’s the wrong one to tell here
If you zoom out to the whole market since 2023, prices for a fixed level of capability have collapsed. Frontier-model output pricing is down roughly 94.5% since March 2023, and a GPT-4-grade model that opened at $30/$60 per million input/output tokens in 2023 now has comparable-capability competition well under $1 per million (Epoch AI). That story is real, and it’s the one you’ve probably already heard.
The story we want to tell is narrower and, we’d argue, more useful if you’re actually running a bill every month: what happens to the price of the same tier, from the same provider, release over release. That’s the number that actually shows up on your invoice when a model you rely on gets replaced by its successor. And on that basis, the trend genuinely does point up.
Same tier, same provider, going up
Start with OpenAI’s flagship line. Standard-tier pricing (confirmed directly against OpenAI’s own pricing page) doubled between GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.5/5.6, from $2.50/$15 to $5/$30 per million input/output tokens — inside less than a year of releases.
Google’s Flash tier tells an even sharper story, because Flash is supposed to be the budget option. Gemini 1.5 Flash launched in May 2024 at $0.15/$0.60, cut a few months later to $0.075/$0.30 (Google Developers Blog). From there: 2.0 Flash at $0.10/$0.40 (pricepertoken.com), 2.5 Flash at $0.15/$1.25 (OpenRouter), 3 Flash Preview at $0.25/$1.50 (pricepertoken.com). Output price alone is up roughly 5x across four generations in about 20 months — call it every 6 to 9 months per release. Even the “cheap” tier isn’t cheap in the way it used to be.
Gemini’s Pro tier moved too: 2.5 Pro launched at $1.25/$10, and 3.1 Pro sits at $2/$12 — about a 60% jump in under a year (CloudZero).
Not every provider is playing this the same way. Anthropic’s Sonnet tier has been remarkably flat — $3/$15 at launch for 3.5 Sonnet in mid-2024, and $3/$15 for Sonnet 4.5 and 4.6 today, confirmed against Anthropic’s own pricing docs. Sonnet 5 is even launching below that, at an introductory $2/$10 through August 2026, before stepping back up to the same $3/$15. Worth a caveat, though: Sonnet’s newer tokenizer produces about 30% more tokens for the same piece of text than the previous one did, so the sticker price staying flat doesn’t necessarily mean your actual bill does.
[Aemond: I’d call this the industry’s version of “we didn’t raise the price, we just made the portion smaller” — the number on the menu is identical, and yet.]
Why: it starts with the metal, not the model
Underneath the API price is a supply chain that’s tight at nearly every layer. Training a frontier model is genuinely brutal — GPT-4 alone ran on an estimated 13 trillion tokens across roughly 25,000 A100 GPUs for about 100 days, with compute costs estimated at $63–78 million before you count staff and R&D (SemiAnalysis). That kind of spend only happens because the chips it depends on are themselves scarce and getting more expensive. NVIDIA’s fiscal 2025 revenue hit $130.5 billion, up 114% year over year, with Data Center revenue — the GPUs actually running these models — up 142% to $115.2 billion (SEC filing, Q4 FY25). And behind NVIDIA sits TSMC, whose advanced nodes (5nm and below) made up 74% of its revenue in Q3 2025, with 3nm and 5nm capacity reported as effectively fully booked into 2026 and prices for sub-5nm chips rising 3–5% for the year — because there’s genuinely nowhere else to go for chips at that process scale (TrendForce, Tom’s Hardware). Every layer of that stack is a bottleneck feeding the next one. [Aemond: it’s a little wild that the entire industry’s price floor ultimately traces back to how many fabs in one part of the world can etch a chip below 5 nanometers. Every “AI is getting cheaper” headline is downstream of a physical process with a handful of operators on the planet.]
That’s also why the shift away from NVIDIA is happening in slow motion rather than all at once. Google’s TPUs and Groq’s chips exist precisely because staying dependent on CUDA is a long-term risk, but building and scaling an alternative is a multi-year, capital-intensive bet — not something a provider can just decide to do this quarter.
The part that actually explains the API tiers
This is where the demand story from the top of this piece comes back in, but sharper. OpenAI and Google have both built explicit Priority and Flex tiers into their pricing: Priority processing runs at a real premium over Standard for lower, more consistent latency, while Flex trades speed for a discount closer to batch pricing (OpenAI, Google). That’s the market pricing patience directly: if you want a guaranteed fast lane, you pay for it; if you can wait, you don’t. [Aemond: airlines figured this out decades ago with boarding groups — the twist here is that the “economy seat” is a queue you can’t see, so most people don’t even realize they’re in one until Priority processing shows up on the pricing page as the alternative.]
But there’s a second, quieter force pushing prices up that has nothing to do with chip scarcity: you’re getting better at this.
You’re the reason too
Training and running these models is a sink that providers need to recoup — that’s standard CapEx logic, no different from any other infrastructure-heavy business. The catch is that the usual way you’d expect that recoup to happen (usage grows, so does revenue) is being undercut by the same users getting more efficient. Early on, most people were asking simple questions and burning tokens accordingly. Now practitioners are learning to do more with less: tools like Caveman, a skill that compresses agent output into terse, low-token phrasing (claims of 65–75% savings, though independent tests on real agentic workflows have found the gains much smaller in practice), or Graphify, which builds a navigable knowledge graph of a codebase so an agent can pull exactly the context it needs instead of re-reading whole files — plus plain old better context management and prompting habits.
If the same amount of user spend now buys fewer tokens per session, and the provider still needs to hit the same revenue targets, raising the per-token price is the straightforward lever. It’s not a conspiracy — it’s the same logic as any business whose customers just got better at using less of the product per dollar of value delivered. [Aemond: worth sitting with — the more competent the industry gets at using this stuff efficiently, the more the industry has an incentive to make efficiency worth less per token.] And there’s a second pressure stacked on top: when a provider’s frontier model becomes the one everyone else is racing to catch — the way Claude Fable 5 has for Anthropic — the rest of the field chasing it only adds more upward pressure of its own. Nobody wants to be the “cheap but behind” option for long.
What that means if you’re the one paying the bill
None of this is really “prices always go up” or “prices always go down” — both are true, depending on what you’re measuring against. Zoom out to the whole market and the story is falling costs. Zoom into any one provider’s flagship or budget tier, release over release, and the story reverses.
So if you’re the one actually watching a monthly bill: don’t treat this quarter’s per-token rate as a stable baseline. Watch the tier, not just the model — a “Flash” or “mini” option two generations from now may not be anywhere near as cheap as the one you’re using today. And if you notice your own usage getting leaner — fewer tokens for the same result, thanks to better prompting, better context management, or tools built specifically to trim the fat — take it as an early signal, not just a win. That’s often exactly the kind of shift that shows up as a price increase on the next release, not the one you just optimized against.
Glossary

• Batch API — A discounted way to submit large volumes of requests that don’t need an instant answer; usually processed within a set window (often 24 hours) at a lower price than normal.

• CapEx (capital expenditure) — Big upfront spending on infrastructure — training runs, data centers, chips — that a company expects to earn back over time, rather than a cost that scales cleanly with each individual sale.

• Context window — The maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) a model can “see” at once in a single request, including everything you send it and everything it writes back.

• Flex processing — A cheaper way to run requests in exchange for slower, best-effort response times — good for tasks that aren’t time-sensitive.

• Frontier model — Whatever’s currently at the very top of a given provider’s lineup — the most capable model they offer, usually also the most expensive.

• Inference — The actual act of running a trained model to produce an answer, as opposed to training it in the first place. Every time you send a prompt and get a response, that’s inference.

• Node (chip manufacturing) — A generation of chipmaking technology, measured in nanometers (e.g., “5nm”); smaller numbers generally mean more powerful, efficient chips, and fewer companies in the world can manufacture at the smallest, most advanced nodes.

• Priority processing — A premium-priced option for guaranteed faster, more consistent response times, as opposed to standard queuing.

• Standard tier — A provider’s normal, default pricing for a model, without any of the speed/latency trade-offs Priority or Flex processing involve.

• Token — The basic unit AI models process text in — roughly three-quarters (3/4) of a word on average, though it varies by language and content. Pricing is quoted per million tokens.

• Tokenizer — The specific method a model uses to break text into tokens. Different tokenizers can produce different token counts for the exact same piece of text, which affects your actual bill even if the per-token price hasn’t changed.
